Guided trip

A dark sky

Your sky from a city, a town and a dark place. It moves the clock to tonight.

Open the trip: A dark sky

The Earth at night

This is the night side of the Earth, and every glow on it is a town. Some of that light never reaches a street. It goes up, or sideways, and lights the air. More than eight people in ten now live under a sky polluted by light.

Your own sky, tonight

Here is your part of the world as tonight's dark arrives. We are going down to the ground to look up at one patch of sky, three times. First as a city shows it, then from a town's edge, then from somewhere properly dark.

From a city

From the middle of a city, only the brightest stars get through, with the planets and the Moon. The sky itself glows. Whatever lies behind that glow is still there, every night. It is only outshone.

From the edge of a town

Away from the centre, the same patch of sky holds many more stars, and the figures of the constellations fill in. Low down there is still a dome of light over the place you left.

From a dark place

Far from any town, on a night with no Moon, there are more stars than you can count, and they lie thickest along one band of the sky. That band is the Milky Way: our own galaxy, seen from inside. One person in three alive today cannot see it from where they live.

What the light costs

It is not only the stars. Birds that travel at night are drawn towards lights, young turtles crawl towards streets instead of the sea, and it is bad for our own health. The night sky has been getting nearly a tenth brighter every year. But this pollution is gone the moment a lamp is shaded or switched off.

How to find the dark

Look at the lights around your own place, and pick a gap between them. Go there in the week around new Moon, when the Moon is out of the evening sky. Give your eyes half an hour in the dark, without a screen, and look up.

Everything is drawn where it really is, from the planets’ own orbits (astronomy-engine).
